items.en: The Root World: Initial Thought Through the Eight Marks
items.zh: 通明觀 · 根本世間 · 覺支

zh: 第二、明釋成覺觀五支之相，即為五：第一、釋覺支，經說覺支云：「覺、大覺，思惟、大思惟，觀於心性。」約此五句以明覺相。今先釋「覺、大覺」二句，此約世間、出世間境界分別，故有此二覺之異。世間境，即是異相；出世間境，即是如相。此之如、異，即是真、俗二諦之別名也。今約觀門，淺深易見。今當具依《摩訶衍》分別。論云：「有三種：上、中、下。」如、異既有三種覺，大覺亦應為三也。論意分別假名為異。分別四大實法同體，名為下如。分別地大異餘三大，名為異。同一無常，生滅不異，名次如。無常生滅，名為異。生滅即空無異，名上如。今即約禪為下、中、上品，明觀門淺深之相。
en: Second, explaining and completing the mark of the five factors, initial thought, sustained reflection, and the rest: this itself has five parts. First, explaining the factor of initial thought — the sūtra, in speaking of the factor of initial thought, says: "Initial thought, great initial thought; deliberation, great deliberation; contemplating the nature of mind." With reference to these five phrases, the mark of initial thought is now clarified.

Here, the first two phrases, "initial thought, great initial thought," are first explained — these are distinguished with reference to the mundane and the world-transcending states, and so this twofold distinction of initial thought and great initial thought arises accordingly. The mundane state is precisely the mark of difference; the world-transcending state is precisely the mark of suchness. This very pair, suchness and difference, is itself simply another name for the two truths, ultimate and conventional. Discussed with reference to the contemplation-gate, this may be readily seen in its shallowness and depth. This shall now be distinguished in full accordance with the Mahāyāna treatise.

The treatise says: "There are three grades: upper, middle, and lower." Since suchness and difference are thus of three grades, initial thought and great initial thought, too, should correspondingly be of three grades. The treatise's own intent distinguishes the provisional name as difference. Distinguishing the four elements' own real dharma as sharing a single substance is named the lower grade of suchness; distinguishing the earth element as different from the other three elements is named difference. Recognizing them as alike impermanent, their arising and ceasing not different from one another, is named the middle grade of suchness; impermanent arising and ceasing itself is named difference. Recognizing that this very arising and ceasing is itself empty, without any difference at all, is named the upper grade of suchness. Here, then, with reference to dhyāna, the lower, middle, and upper grades are distinguished, clarifying the mark of the contemplation-gate's own shallowness and depth.

zh: 第一、先明下品覺相。覺氣息入出，青、黃、赤、白諸色隔別，名為覺；覺此諸息同一風大無異，名大覺。次覺三十六物隔別，名為覺；覺餘三大無有別異，名大覺。覺於心數非一，名為覺；同是四心無異，名大覺。第二、明中品覺者，息是風大，名為覺；覺息生滅無常，名大覺。覺餘三大各別，名為覺；覺同一無常，生滅不異，名大覺。覺四心差別不同，名為覺；覺無常生滅不異，名大覺。
en: First, clarifying beforehand the mark of the lower grade of initial thought: perceiving the breath entering and leaving, its various colors, blue, yellow, red, white, each distinct from the other, this is named initial thought; perceiving all these breaths as sharing, without difference, the single element of wind, this is named great initial thought. Next, perceiving the thirty-six substances as each distinct from the other, this is named initial thought; perceiving the remaining three elements as without any distinction between them, this is named great initial thought. Perceiving the mental factors as not of one kind only, this is named initial thought; perceiving them as, alike, these same four states of mind, without difference, this is named great initial thought.

Second, clarifying the mark of the middle grade of initial thought: recognizing the breath as the element of wind, this is named initial thought; perceiving the breath's own arising and ceasing as impermanent, this is named great initial thought. Perceiving the remaining three elements as each distinct, this is named initial thought; perceiving them as alike impermanent, their arising and ceasing not different from one another, this is named great initial thought. Perceiving the four states of mind as differing from one another, this is named initial thought; perceiving their impermanent arising and ceasing as not different from one another, this is named great initial thought.

zh: 第三、明上品覺者，覺息無常為異者，此息為八相所遷，故無常。何等為八相？一、生；二、住；三、異；四、滅；五、生生；六、住住；七、異異；八、滅滅。此八種相遷法體別異非一，名為覺；覺息本空寂，無八相之異，名大覺。覺餘三大各有八相別異，名為覺；覺餘三大本來空寂，無八相之異，名大覺。覺心八相所遷，別異非一，名為覺；覺心本來空寂，無八相之異，名大覺。
en: Third, clarifying the mark of the upper grade of initial thought: perceiving the breath's own impermanence as difference — this breath is shifted by eight marks, and so is impermanent. What are these eight marks? Arising; abiding; changing; ceasing; the arising of arising; the abiding of abiding; the changing of changing; and the ceasing of ceasing. These eight kinds of mark, shifting the dharma's own substance, distinct from one another, not of one kind only, this is named initial thought; perceiving the breath as originally empty and still, without any of these eight marks' own difference at all, this is named great initial thought.

Perceiving the remaining three elements as each having these eight marks' own distinction, this is named initial thought; perceiving the remaining three elements as originally empty and still, without any of these eight marks' own difference at all, this is named great initial thought. Perceiving the mind as shifted by these eight marks, distinct from one another, not of one kind only, this is named initial thought; perceiving the mind as originally empty and still, without any of these eight marks' own difference at all, this is named great initial thought.

zh: 所以者何？若心即是八相，八相即是心者，則壞有餘相。所以者何？今息色亦即是八相，八相亦即是息色，八相無異故，息、色、心三事亦應無異。若爾，說心時，即應是說息、色。今實不爾，壞亂世諦相故。如人喚火，應得水來。說心一向即是息、色，過同於此。復次，若離心有八相，離八相有心者，此則心非八相，八相非心。若心非八相，則心但有名無相，無相之法，是不名心。若八相離心，八相則無所遷，即不名八相，八相無所相故。如是審諦求之，則心與八相本自不有，亦不依他有性，性如虛空，無一異相，故名大覺。覺前息、色一一亦當如是分別。此則略說上品覺、大覺之相。
en: Why is this? Were the mind itself identical to these eight marks, and these eight marks identical to the mind, this would destroy the marks of the others. Why is this? Here, the breath and form, too, would then be identical to these eight marks, and these eight marks identical to the breath and form — and, the eight marks being without difference, the breath, form, and mind, these three matters, ought then to be without difference from one another as well. If this were so, then, whenever mind is spoken of, one ought equally to be speaking of breath and form — but this is, in truth, not so at all, since it would destroy the very mark of conventional truth. It is like calling for fire and expecting water to come instead. To say that mind is, without exception, identical to breath and form suffers from exactly this same fault.

Furthermore: were the eight marks present apart from mind, and mind present apart from the eight marks, then mind would not be the eight marks, and the eight marks would not be mind. If mind is not the eight marks, then mind would have only a name, without any mark at all, and a dharma without any mark cannot properly be named "mind" at all. If the eight marks are apart from mind, then the eight marks would have nothing to shift, and so could not properly be named "the eight marks" either, since the eight marks would then have nothing that they mark at all. Examined and sought after closely in this way, mind and the eight marks are, in themselves, originally without existence at all, nor do they possess any nature dependent on anything else either — their nature is like empty space itself, without any mark of either sameness or difference — hence this is named great initial thought. The breath and form already discussed should likewise, each in turn, be distinguished in this same way. This, in brief, describes the mark of the upper grade of initial thought and great initial thought.

The eight marks of conditioned existence (arising, abiding, changing, ceasing, and each of these four applied a second time, to itself) is a classical Abhidharma scheme for how a moment of existence is not simply born and destroyed but shepherded through its own life-cycle by four further, second-order marks — here used to give the upper grade of initial thought a genuinely rigorous object. The refutation of "mind simply is the eight marks" versus "mind is entirely separate from the eight marks" refutes the two extremes of identity and separation, this time protecting a middle position: mind and its impermanence-marks are neither identical (which would collapse mind into breath and form, "calling for fire and expecting water") nor separate (which would leave both mind and the marks without any coherent referent at all), but empty of fixed existence in exactly the same way, "like empty space itself."

通明觀 · 根本世間 · 覺支

zh: 次釋「思惟、大思惟」二句。此還約前覺、大覺說。所以者何？初心覺悟真俗之相，名覺、大覺；後心重慮觀察，名思惟、大思惟。對小覺後說思惟，大覺後說大思惟，此義易見，不煩多釋。次釋「觀於心性」者，即是返觀能思惟、大思惟之心也。所以者何？行者雖能了於前境，而不能返達觀心，則不會實道。今即返照能觀之心，為從觀心生，為從非觀心生？若從觀心生，若從非觀心生，二俱有過，當知觀心畢竟空寂。五句釋覺支竟。
en: Next, explaining the two phrases "deliberation, great deliberation." These, too, are explained with reference to the initial thought and great initial thought already given. Why is this? The initial mind's own awakening to the mark of the ultimate and conventional is named initial thought and great initial thought; the later mind's own repeated deliberation and observation of this is named deliberation and great deliberation. Deliberation is spoken of following the lesser initial thought, and great deliberation following the great initial thought — this sense is readily seen, and need not be explained further here.

Next, explaining "contemplating the nature of mind": this is precisely turning the contemplation back upon the very mind that does this deliberating and great deliberating. Why is this? The practitioner, though able to fully understand the object before them, if unable to turn back and directly contemplate the contemplating mind itself, will fail to meet the true path. Here, then, one turns the contemplation back upon the very mind doing the observing: does it arise from a contemplating mind, or from a non-contemplating mind? Whether it arises from a contemplating mind or from a non-contemplating mind, both alternatives carry their own fault — one should know, then, that the contemplating mind is, in the end, empty and still. This concludes the five phrases explaining the factor of initial thought.

zh: 第二、次釋觀支。經云：「若觀心行、大行、遍行、隨意。」觀心者，即是前觀於心性也。行、大行者，聲聞之人以四諦為大行，當觀心時，即具四諦正觀。所以者何？若人不了心故無明，不了造諸結業，名為集諦。集諦因緣，必招未來名色苦果，是名苦諦。若觀心性，即是具足戒、定、智慧，行三十七品，故名道諦。若有正道，則現在煩惱不生，未來苦果亦滅，名為滅諦。是名聲聞大行。若緣覺人，以十二因緣為大行。若是菩薩，即入無生正道正觀，證於寂定瑠璃三昧，毛孔見佛，入菩薩位也。則略明三乘大行之道相也。
en: Second, next explaining the factor of sustained reflection. The sūtra says: "Observing mind; conduct, great conduct, pervasive conduct, and conduct at will." "Observing mind" is precisely the same as "contemplating the nature of mind" already given above.

As for "conduct" and "great conduct": the śrāvaka takes the Four Noble Truths as great conduct — at the very moment mind is observed, one is already complete with the right contemplation of the Four Noble Truths. Why is this? If a person, failing to understand mind, thereby remains in ignorance, and, not understanding this, creates every kind of fettering karma, this is named the truth of accumulation. The causes and conditions of this accumulation are bound to bring about the future's own painful result of name-and-form — this is named the truth of suffering. Contemplating the nature of mind is itself already complete with moral discipline, concentration, and wisdom, practicing the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment — hence this is named the truth of the path. Where there is this right path, present affliction no longer arises, and the future's own painful result is thereby extinguished as well — this is named the truth of cessation. This is the śrāvaka's own great conduct. The pratyekabuddha, by contrast, takes the twelve links of dependent origination as great conduct. And the bodhisattva enters directly into the right path and right contemplation of the unarisen, realizing the still concentration of the lapis-lazuli samādhi, seeing the Buddha through every pore, entering the bodhisattva's own stage. This, in brief, clarifies the mark of the three vehicles' own path of great conduct.

zh: 遍行者，觀行未利，亦並約心而觀四諦，名為大行。今觀道稍利，能遍歷諸緣，觀於四諦，出十六行觀，故名遍行。隨意者，若是遍行，雖在定內，得見諸緣，出禪定時，則觀不相應。今隨意者，隨出入定，觀一切法，任運自成，不由作意，是名隨意。此則略釋觀支相也。
en: As for "pervasive conduct": when one's contemplative practice is not yet sharp, one still, alike, contemplates the Four Noble Truths with reference to mind alone — this is named great conduct. Here, once the path of contemplation has grown somewhat sharper, one is able to range pervasively through every condition, contemplating the Four Noble Truths, bringing forth the sixteen aspects of contemplation — hence this is named pervasive conduct. As for "conduct at will": within pervasive conduct, although one is able to see every condition while still within concentration, upon emerging from dhyāna-concentration, this contemplation no longer corresponds. Here, "at will" means that, whether entering or emerging from concentration, one contemplates every dharma whatsoever, spontaneously accomplished of its own accord, not dependent on any deliberate intention at all — this is named conduct at will. This, in brief, explains the mark of the factor of sustained reflection.

zh: 第三、明喜支。喜支者，經言：「如真實知、大知，心動至心，是名為喜。」如真實知者，即是上來觀於心性四諦真理也。大知者，如上觀行。若心審諦，停住緣內，稱觀而知，故言如真實知。若豁然開悟，稱理而知，心生法喜，故名大知。心動至心者，既得法喜心動，若隨此喜，則為顛倒。今了此喜無，即得喜性。即得喜性故，名至心，是名為喜。
en: Third, clarifying the factor of joy. The sūtra says: "Suchness-knowledge, great knowledge; the mind moved all the way to the very heart of mind itself — this is named joy." "Suchness-knowledge" is precisely the true principle of the Four Noble Truths within contemplating the nature of mind, already given above. "Great knowledge" is as within the contemplative practice already given above. If the mind closely examines and dwells within its object, knowing in accordance with contemplation, this is called suchness-knowledge. If one suddenly awakens, knowing in accordance with principle, the mind giving rise to the joy of the Dharma, this is named great knowledge. "The mind moved all the way to the very heart of mind itself" means that, having attained the joy of the Dharma, the mind is moved by it, and, were one to simply follow along with this joy, this would be a form of inversion. Here, understanding that this very joy is without existence, one thereby attains joy's own true nature, and, having attained joy's own true nature, this is named "all the way to the very heart of mind" — this is named joy.

zh: 第四、次明安支。安支者，經言：「若身安、心安、受安，受於樂觸，是名為安。」身安者，了達身性故，不為身業所動，即得身安，故名身安。心安者，了達心性故，不為心業所動，即得心樂，故名心安。受安者，能觀之心，名之為受，知受非受，斷諸受故，名之為樂，故名受安。受於樂觸者，世間、出世間二種樂法成就，樂法對心，故受於樂。第五、次明定支者，經言：「若心住、大住，不亂於緣，不謬，無有顛倒，是名為定。」心住者，住世間定法，持心不散，故名住。大住者，住真如定法，持心不散故。
en: Fourth, next clarifying the factor of ease. The sūtra says: "Ease of body, ease of mind, and ease of sensation, receiving a blissful touch — this is named ease." "Ease of body" means that, having fully understood the body's own nature, one is no longer moved by any bodily karma, and thereby attains bodily ease — hence this is named ease of body. "Ease of mind" means that, having fully understood the mind's own nature, one is no longer moved by any mental karma, and thereby attains mental happiness — hence this is named ease of mind. "Ease of sensation" means that the very mind able to observe is itself named "sensation" — knowing sensation as not truly "sensation" at all, severing every such sensation, this is named "happiness" — hence this is named ease of sensation. "Receiving a blissful touch" means that both the mundane and world-transcending kinds of blissful dharma have been accomplished, this blissful dharma meeting the mind directly — hence one receives this very bliss.

Fifth, next clarifying the factor of concentration. The sūtra says: "The mind abiding, greatly abiding, undisturbed by any object, unmistaken, free of any inversion whatsoever — this is named concentration." "The mind abiding" means abiding in the mundane dharma of concentration, sustaining the mind without scattering — hence this is named abiding. "Greatly abiding" means abiding in the dharma of concentration that is true suchness itself, sustaining the mind without scattering.

zh: 不亂於緣者，雖住一心，而分別世間之相不亂也。不謬者，謬名妄謬，諦了真如，妄取不起，故言不謬。不顛倒者，若心偏取世間相，即隨有見沈沒生死，不得解脫。若心偏取如相，即隨空見，破世間因果，不修善法，是大可畏處。行者善達真、俗，離此二種邪命，名不顛倒。復次，若二乘之人得此心，破四倒，名不顛倒。若是菩薩得此一心，能破八倒，名不顛倒。行者初得覺支成就，即覺身息不實，猶如芭蕉。今得住此一心，定支成就。心既寂靜，於後泯然微細，即覺身息之相不實，猶如聚沫。是則略明下根行者證通明初禪之相。
en: "Undisturbed by any object" means that, although abiding single-mindedly, one's discrimination of the mundane world's own marks remains undisturbed. "Unmistaken" means free of the fault of deluded mistake — closely understanding true suchness, deluded grasping no longer arises — hence this is called unmistaken. "Free of any inversion" means: were the mind to lean one-sidedly toward grasping the mundane world's own mark, one would then follow the view of existence, sinking into birth-and-death, unable to attain liberation; and were the mind to lean one-sidedly toward grasping the mark of suchness instead, one would then follow the view of emptiness, breaking apart the mundane world's own cause and effect, no longer cultivating any wholesome dharma at all — this is a place of great peril. The practitioner, properly penetrating both the ultimate and the conventional, leaving behind these two deviant modes of livelihood, this is named free of inversion. Furthermore: should a practitioner of the two lesser vehicles attain this very mind, breaking through the four inversions, this, too, is named free of inversion; and should a bodhisattva attain this same single mind, able to break through the eight inversions, this, too, is named free of inversion.

The practitioner, first attaining the accomplishment of the factor of initial thought, perceives the body and breath as unreal, just like a plantain trunk. Now, abiding in this very single-pointed mind, the factor of concentration, too, is accomplished. The mind now still, afterward growing indistinct and fine, one perceives the mark of body and breath as unreal, just like a mass of foam. This, in brief, clarifies the mark of a practitioner of lower faculty realizing the thorough-and-bright contemplation's first dhyāna.

The five factors here map onto a familiar structure (initial thought, sustained reflection, joy, ease, concentration parallel the first dhyāna's own覺觀喜樂一心 from fascicle 5) but each is redefined around insight rather than raw absorption — sustained reflection becomes an explicit walk through the "great conduct" of each of the three vehicles (the Four Noble Truths for śrāvakas, the twelve links for pratyekabuddhas, entry into the unarisen for bodhisattvas), joy becomes the recognition that joy itself "is without existence," and concentration's own "freedom from inversion" is calibrated by vehicle, four inversions broken for the two lesser vehicles and eight for the bodhisattva. This entire elaborate five-factor, eight-marks analysis, spanning several pages of source text, is explicitly said to describe only "a practitioner of lower faculty" — the treatise is about to walk through this same first dhyāna two more times, at increasing depth, for the middle and upper faculties.

quiz.q: What are the five phrases of the factor of initial thought?
options: initial thought, great initial thought, deliberation, great deliberation, contemplating the nature of mind
quiz.why: The five phrases are initial thought, great initial thought, deliberation, great deliberation, and contemplating the nature of mind.

quiz.q: Of what are "suchness" and "difference" other names?
options: the two truths: the world-transcending is suchness, the mundane is difference
quiz.why: The mundane state is the mark of difference and the world-transcending state the mark of suchness; suchness and difference are other names for the two truths.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, what are the lower, middle, and upper suchness?
options: the four elements sharing one substance; alike impermanent; arising and ceasing itself empty
quiz.why: The four elements sharing one real substance is lower suchness; all alike impermanent is middle suchness; arising and ceasing as empty without difference is upper suchness.

quiz.q: In the lower grade, what are initial thought and great initial thought?
options: the breaths' colors as distinct is initial thought; all as one wind element is great initial thought
quiz.why: In the lower grade, seeing the breaths' colors as distinct is initial thought; seeing them all as one wind element is great initial thought. B is the middle grade; C and D the upper.

quiz.q: In the middle grade, what are initial thought and great initial thought regarding the breath?
options: the breath as wind is initial thought; its impermanent arising and ceasing is great initial thought
quiz.why: In the middle grade, recognizing the breath as wind is initial thought; perceiving its impermanent arising and ceasing is great initial thought.

quiz.q: In the upper grade, the breath is shifted by eight marks. What are they?
options: arising, abiding, changing, ceasing, and the arising of arising, abiding of abiding, changing of changing, ceasing of ceasing
birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, grief, pain, distress
quiz.why: The eight are arising, abiding, changing, ceasing, and the arising of arising, abiding of abiding, changing of changing, and ceasing of ceasing.

quiz.q: In the upper grade, what are initial thought and great initial thought?
options: the eight marks shifting the breath as distinct is initial thought; the breath as originally empty without them is great initial thought
quiz.why: Seeing the eight marks shift the breath's substance, distinct and many, is initial thought; seeing the breath as originally empty, without the eight marks' difference, is great initial thought.

quiz.q: What fault follows from saying mind is identical to the eight marks, and what comparison is given?
options: breath and form would also be the eight marks, so the three would be identical, destroying conventional truth, like calling for fire and getting water
quiz.why: If the eight marks are identical with mind, and also with breath and form, the three would not differ, and speaking of mind would be speaking of breath, destroying conventional truth, like calling for fire and getting water.

quiz.q: What fault follows from saying the eight marks exist apart from mind?
options: mind without marks is a name only and not mind; marks without mind shift nothing and are not marks
quiz.why: If mind is not the eight marks, it has a name but no mark and cannot be called mind; if the marks are apart from mind, they shift nothing and cannot be called marks.

quiz.q: How do deliberation and great deliberation relate to initial thought and great initial thought?
options: the first mind's awakening is thought; the later mind's repeated examination is deliberation, following each respectively
quiz.why: The first mind awakening to the two truths is initial and great initial thought; the later mind's repeated deliberation is deliberation and great deliberation, following each in turn.

quiz.q: What is "contemplating the nature of mind," and why is it necessary?
options: turning back on the deliberating mind; without this one misses the true path; whether from a contemplating or non-contemplating mind, it is empty
quiz.why: It turns back on the deliberating mind; understanding objects without turning back fails to meet the true path. Whether it arises from a contemplating or non-contemplating mind, both fail, so it is empty.

quiz.q: What does each of the three vehicles take as "great conduct"?
options: śrāvakas the Four Truths; pratyekabuddhas the twelve links; bodhisattvas enter the unarisen, realizing the lapis samādhi and seeing buddhas through the pores
quiz.why: Śrāvakas take the Four Noble Truths, pratyekabuddhas the twelve links, and bodhisattvas enter the unarisen, realizing the lapis-lazuli samādhi and seeing buddhas through every pore.

quiz.q: How are "pervasive conduct" and "conduct at will" distinguished?
options: pervasive: ranging through every condition with the sixteen aspects; at will: contemplating in and out of concentration spontaneously
quiz.why: Pervasive conduct ranges through all conditions, producing the sixteen aspects, but fails outside concentration; conduct at will contemplates every dharma whether entering or leaving concentration, spontaneously.

quiz.q: In the factor of joy, how are suchness-knowledge and great knowledge distinguished?
options: knowing in accord with contemplation is suchness-knowledge; sudden awakening in accord with principle, with Dharma-joy, is great knowledge
quiz.why: Closely examining and dwelling on the object, knowing in accord with contemplation, is suchness-knowledge; suddenly awakening in accord with principle, with Dharma-joy, is great knowledge.

quiz.q: How is "the mind moved to the very mind" explained?
options: Dharma-joy moves the mind; following it is inversion; seeing it as without existence one attains joy's nature, called reaching the mind
quiz.why: Dharma-joy stirs the mind; following it is inversion. Understanding the joy as without existence, one attains its nature, which is "reaching the mind."

options: the observing mind is called sensation; knowing it is not sensation and severing sensations is happiness
quiz.why: The observing mind is called sensation; knowing it is not truly sensation and severing sensations is happiness, hence ease of sensation.

quiz.q: In the factor of concentration, "free of inversion" means avoiding which two one-sided graspings?
options: grasping the mundane leads to the view of existence; grasping suchness leads to the view of emptiness, destroying cause and effect
quiz.why: Grasping the mundane leads to the view of existence and sinking in birth and death; grasping suchness leads to the view of emptiness, destroying worldly cause and effect. Penetrating both truths avoids both.

quiz.q: When the factor of initial thought and the factor of concentration are each accomplished, how are body and breath perceived?
options: with initial thought, like a plantain; with concentration, like a mass of foam
quiz.why: With initial thought accomplished, body and breath are like a plantain; with concentration accomplished, like a mass of foam. Bubble, cloud, and shadow belong to the second through fourth dhyānas.
